The BRDM-2 is a Russian armored reconnaissance vehicle. It was developed in the Soviet Union in the early 1950s.
Its armament consists of a 14.5 mm KPVT heavy machine gun and a 7.62 mm PKT coaxial machine gun,
identical to the Russian armored personnel carriers BTR-60/BTR-70/BTR-80.
The BRDM-2, in various versions, is used by the armed forces of over 50 countries worldwide.
Entered service in 1962.
Crew: 4.

The BRM-1K is a Russian armored reconnaissance vehicle. It was developed from the BMP-1 infantry fighting vehicle in the 1970s.
It has the same architecture as the BMP-1 with the engine at the front right and the driver's position at the front left.
The BRM-1K received a new two-seat turret unlike the single-seat turret of the BMP-1.
The armament consists of the 73 mm 2A28 Grom gun, identical to the BMP-1.
Cannon: 73 mm 2A28 Grom.
Crew: 6.

The BRM-3K Rys (Lynx in Russian) is a Russian armored reconnaissance vehicle, entered service in 1995.
It is developed on the chassis of the BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicle for reconnaissance units.
Its missions are: observation, target detection, determining position of detected targets and transmitting intelligence to higher echelons.
The BRM-3K is equipped with a 1RL-133-3 ground Doppler radar, laser rangefinder, thermal camera,
navigation system, data transmission system at a distance of 100 km while moving and 350 km stationary.
Cannon: 30 mm.
Crew: 3 + 3.

The FV107 Scimitar is a British armored reconnaissance vehicle, entered service in 1971.\nIt is equipped with a two-seat turret armed with a 30 mm L21 Rarden automatic cannon and a 7.62 mm coaxial machine gun.\nCrew: 3.

The BMP-1 is a Russian infantry fighting vehicle, entered service in 1966.
It is the first vehicle of its category, developed to enhance the capabilities of mechanized infantry units.
The BMP-1 is an amphibious vehicle capable of operating in NBC environment.
Its crew consists of the commander, gunner, driver and eight infantrymen.
The BMP-1 has a single-seat turret armed with a 73 mm 2A28 Grom smoothbore cannon,
a 7.62 mm PKTM coaxial machine gun and the 9M14M Malyutka anti-tank missile, AT-3 Sagger.
Infantrymen can fire from inside the vehicle through nine firing ports.
Between 1966 and 1988, over 20,000 BMP-1s were built. In August 2018, a new version of the BMP-1 was presented as BMP-1AM Basurmanin.
Crew: 3 + 8.

The BMP-2 is a Russian infantry fighting vehicle, entered service in 1981.
It is developed on the chassis of the BMP-1 infantry fighting vehicle.
The powertrain is at the front right and the driver's position at the front left. It is amphibious and NBC protected.
To improve its firepower, the BMP-2 receives a two-seat turret, armed with a 30 mm 2A42 automatic cannon,
a 7.62 mm PKT coaxial machine gun and anti-tank missiles.
Adopted by many armies worldwide.
Crew: 3 + 7.

The BMP-3 is a Russian infantry fighting vehicle, entered service in 1987.
It is the most heavily armed vehicle in its category.
Its armament consists of a 100 mm 2A70 low-pressure gun, a 30 mm 2A72 automatic cannon,
a 7.62 mm PKT coaxial machine gun.
The BMP-3 can fire through the 100 mm gun the 9M117 anti-tank missile of the 9K166-3 Basnya system, AT-12 Swinger.
The BMP-3 chassis adopts the configuration of the Russian paratroopers' BMD combat vehicle family.
Crew: 3 + 7.

The MTLB is a Russian multi-role armored transport vehicle, entered service in 1964.
It is designed as an artillery gun tractor and equipment transporter.
Later, the MTLB was adopted in troop transport version, medical evacuation vehicle and platform for installing various systems and equipment.
Crew: 2 + 11.

The BMD-1 is a Russian airborne infantry fighting vehicle for paratroop units, entered service in 1969.\nThe single-seat turret is armed with a 73 mm 2A28 Grom cannon, a 7.62 mm PKT coaxial machine gun.\nCrew: 2 + 5.

The BMD-2 is a Russian airborne infantry fighting vehicle for paratroop units, developed in the 1980s.
It is developed from the BMD-1 chassis. It has the new weapon system with a single-seat turret armed with a 30 mm 2A42 cannon
and a 7.62 mm PKT coaxial machine gun.
For anti-tank combat, it is equipped with a system capable of firing 9M111 Fagot AT-4 or 9M113 Konkurs AT-5 anti-tank missiles.
Crew: 2 + 5.

The BMD-3 is a Russian airborne infantry fighting vehicle for paratroop units, entered service in 1990.
It is air-droppable.
Cannon: 30 mm 2A42 x100.2 caliber.
Coaxial machine gun: 7.62 mm PKT.
Hull automatic grenade launcher: 30 mm AG-17.
Crew: 2 + 5.

The BMD-4 is a Russian airborne infantry fighting vehicle for paratroop units, entered service in 2004.
It has the same five-wheel chassis as its predecessor the BMD-3.
The vehicle receives a new Bakhtcha-U turret that significantly increases firepower.
The Bakhtcha-U turret is derived from the weapon system of the BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicle.
Cannon: 100 mm / 30 mm.
Coaxial machine gun: 7.62 mm.
Crew: 2 + 6.

The BTR-60 is a Russian 8×8 wheeled armored personnel carrier, entered service in 1960.
The open-top BTR-60P version transports two crew members and 12 to 14 infantrymen.
The armament consists of a manually operated 12.7 mm machine gun and one or more 7.62 mm machine guns mounted on the sides.
The BTR-60PA version receives a roof and benefits from NBC protection.
The BTR-60PB version is equipped with a single-seat turret armed with a 14.5 mm KPVT heavy machine gun and a 7.62 mm PKT coaxial machine gun.
Very widely exported worldwide.
Crew: 3 + 8.

The BTR-70 is a Russian 8×8 wheeled armored personnel carrier, entered service in 1976.
It has the same architecture as its predecessor the BTR-60.
The BTR-70 version is equipped with a single-seat turret armed with a 14.5 mm KPVT heavy machine gun and a 7.62 mm PKT coaxial machine gun.
Crew: 3 + 7.

The BTR-80 is a Russian 8×8 wheeled armored personnel carrier, entered service in 1986.
It has the same architecture as its predecessor the BTR-70, with the engine at the rear of the vehicle.
Access on board is through double side doors.
Machine gun: 14.5 mm.
Coaxial machine gun: 7.62 mm.
Crew: 3 + 7.

The XA-180 is a Finnish 6×6 wheeled armored personnel carrier, entered service in 1984.
It was developed at the request of the Finnish army to replace the Soviet BTR-60 armored personnel carriers.
The XA-180 is made from the Sisu SA-150 heavy truck.
The XA-180 was developed in several versions and exported to the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia.
The XA-180 in different versions has been deployed in Afghanistan, Bosnia, Iraq, Kosovo, Lebanon, Somalia, Chad.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm or 7.62 mm.
Crew: 2 + 10 to 16.
The TPz1 Fuchs is a German 6×6 wheeled armored personnel carrier, developed in the late 1970s.\nArmament: 7.62 mm machine gun.\nCrew: 2 + 8.

The BMR-600 is a Spanish 6×6 wheeled armored personnel carrier, entered service in 1979.
Nearly 1,500 BMR-600s were produced in different versions.
It was exported to Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Peru.
Armament: 12.7 mm, M2HB.
Crew: 3 + 8.

The Piranha 2 is a Swiss 4x4/6×6/8x8 wheeled armored personnel carrier.
The Piranha 2 was an improved version of MOWAG's successful family of wheeled fighting vehicles.
Can be equipped with a turret, flat-shaped, forming an angle at its base, placed on the left,
in the center of the vehicle roof, with a 12.7 mm machine gun and a 7.62 mm machine gun.
Crew: 3 + 9.

The M1126 Stryker is an American 8×8 wheeled armored personnel carrier, entered service in 2002.
It is developed from the Canadian LAV-III Kodiak based on the Piranha III armored vehicle.
It has the M151 Protector RWS remote turret that can receive a 12.7 mm M2HB heavy machine gun
or a 40 mm Mk 19 automatic grenade launcher.
In June 2021, the US Army selected the Samson remote turret armed with a 30 mm cannon to equip Stryker combat vehicles.
Crew: 2 + 9.

The M113 is an American armored personnel carrier, entered service in 1960.
It was developed for infantry units for transporting an infantry squad.
It has undergone several modernization campaigns.
The M113 is derived into a wide range of specialized vehicles: command post, mortar, medical, air defense,
engineering vehicle, anti-tank missile launcher, etc.
Adopted by numerous armed forces worldwide.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Crew: 2 + 11.

The SPz Marder is a German infantry fighting vehicle, entered service in 1971.
It is equipped with a two-seat turret in superstructure armed with a 20 mm Rh 202 automatic cannon
and a 7.62 mm MG3A1 machine gun.
Delivered to Indonesia, Jordan and Chile.
Crew: 3 + 6 to 7.

The SPz Puma is a German heavy infantry fighting vehicle, developed in the 2000s.
It is developed to replace the SPz Marder in German mechanized infantry units.
The SPz Puma is equipped with a remote turret armed with a 30 mm MK.30-2 cannon and a 5.56 mm coaxial machine gun.
It has two protection levels. Level A, Air-transportable, with complete mine protection and ballistic protection
against 30 mm rounds from the front and 14.5 mm from the side.
Crew: 3 + 6.

The M2A2 Bradley is an American infantry fighting vehicle, entered service in 1981.
It is armed with a 25 mm Bushmaster cannon.
From 1986, the M1A1 model receives two TOW anti-tank missiles.
The M2A2 Bradley has undergone several modernization campaigns improving its combat capabilities, protection level,
mobility and various equipment.
A reconnaissance version is developed as the M3 Bradley.
Crew: 3 + 7.
The MCV-80 Warrior is a British infantry fighting vehicle, entered service in 1987.\nIt is armed with a 30 mm L21A1 Rarden automatic cannon and a 7.62 mm L94A1 coaxial machine gun.\nCrew: 3 + 7.

The BMP-KSHM is an armored command vehicle based on the Russian BMP-1 chassis, entered service in 1972.
For self-defense, the BMP-KSHM is equipped with a 7.62 mm PK machine gun.
Although it retains the standard single-seat turret of the BMP-1, its 76 mm gun has been removed and replaced with a larger telescopic antenna,
called HAWK EYE.
The BMP-1KSh is fully amphibious: its water propulsion is provided by its tracks.
Crew: 3.

The R-142 Deimos is a tactical command and communications vehicle (battalion/regiment level) of Russian ground forces.
It allows establishing bidirectional radio links with homologous stations in all conditions (day/night, all seasons),
stationary and moving (up to 40 km/h).
Operational range: 2000 km in telegraphic mode (auditory reception).
Crew: 3 to 4.

The T-55 is a Russian main battle tank, entered service in 1958.
It is widely distributed worldwide.
It was produced under license in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Romania.
Since entering service, the T-55 has taken part in numerous conflicts.
It remains in service in several armed forces.
Cannon: 100 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Crew: 4.
The T-62 is a Soviet medium tank, entered service in 1961.\nMain armament: 115 mm cannon.\nCrew: 4.

The T-64 is a Soviet main battle tank, entered service in 1965.
It is the first Soviet tank to integrate automatic loading.
Cannon: 125 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Anti-tank missile: AT-8 for T-64B.
Crew: 3.

The T-72 is a Russian main battle tank, entered service in 1973.
Cannon: 125 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Crew: 3.

The T-80 is a Russian main battle tank, developed in the 1980s.
Armament: Cannon - 125 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Crew: 3.

The T-90 is a Russian main battle tank, entered service in 1992.
Armament: Cannon - 125 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Crew: 3.

The T-14 Armata is a Russian main battle tank project, in development since the early 2010s.
It is equipped with an unmanned remote-controlled turret.
All ammunition is stored in the automatic loader installed in the turret well.
The three crew members are placed at the front of the chassis.
Cannon: 125 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm or 7.62 mm.
Serial production launch announced for 2019.
Crew: 3.

The M1A1 Abrams is an American main battle tank, entered service in 1980.
The first M1 Abrams models are equipped with a 105 mm M68 cannon.
From the M1A1 version, it is armed with the 120 mm M256 cannon.
Cannon: 120 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Crew: 4.

The M60 is an American main battle tank, developed in the 1950s.
It was widely exported worldwide.
It is still in service in several armed forces.
Armament: Cannon - 105 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm Browning M2.
Several modernization campaigns: M60A1 (1962), M60A2 (1970), M60A3 (1975).
Crew: 4.

The Leopard 1 is a German main battle tank, entered service in 1965.
It was widely exported worldwide.
Currently, it is in service in Turkey, Brazil and Chile.
From February 2023, Germany delivers Leopard 1 to Ukraine.
The Leopard 1 chassis served as the basis for various support vehicles.
Cannon: 105 mm.
Machine gun: 7.62 mm.
Crew: 4.

The Leopard 2 is a German main battle tank, developed in the 1970s.
Armament: Cannon - 120 mm.
Machine gun: 7.62 mm.
Crew: 4.

The Chieftain is a British main battle tank, entered service in 1966.
It was developed by Leyland Motors.
The Chieftain was employed in British armored units until its replacement by the Challenger 1 main battle tank.
It was exported to Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Jordan and Oman.
In Jordan, it is employed as Khalid and in Iran as Shir.
Armament: Cannon - 120 mm.
Machine gun: 7.62 mm.
Crew: 4.

The Challenger 1 is a British main battle tank, entered service in 1983.
The modernization of Challenger 1 gave birth to Challenger 2.
Cannon: 120 mm.
Machine gun: 7.62 mm.
Crew: 4.

The Challenger 2 is a British main battle tank, entered service in 1998.
It is known as FV4030.
Challenger 2 is the main tank of the British army.
It participated in engagements in Kosovo and Iraq.
The Challenger 2 was exported to Oman in 38 units.
In 2021, the British army will receive 148 modernized tanks as Challenger 3.
Cannon: 120 mm.
Machine gun: 7.62 mm.
Crew: 4.

The C1 Ariete is an Italian main battle tank, entered service in 1995.
Armament: Cannon - 120 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm, 7.62 mm.
Crew: 4.

The Type 98 (ZTZ-98) is a Chinese main battle tank, introduced in 1999 during a military parade in Beijing.
It resembles the T-72, but the turret is welded.
Its main armament is a 125 mm smoothbore cannon.
Crew: 3.

The ZTZ-99 (Type-99) is a Chinese main battle tank, entered service in 2003.
It is equipped with a thermal camera and stabilized panoramic sight of the commander with hunter-killer capability.
The ZTZ-99 is equipped with an omnidirectional laser countermeasure system installed on the turret roof.
Cannon: 125 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Crew: 3.

The Merkava Mk IV is an Israeli main battle tank, entered service in 2004.
The Merkava Mk IV chassis served as the basis for the Namer heavy armored personnel carrier.
Israel is the sole user of the Merkava Mk IV tank.
Cannon: 120 mm.
Machine gun: 7.62 mm/12.7 mm.
Mortar: 60 mm.
Crew: 4.

The PT-91 Twardy is a Polish main battle tank, entered service in 1995.
It is developed by Bumar Labedy from the T-72M1 tank.
The PT-91 Twardy was produced in 232 units for the Polish army needs.
Between 2007 and 2010, it was exported to Malaysia in 48 units as PT-91M Pendekar.
Armament: Cannon - 125 mm.
Coaxial machine gun: 7.62 mm.
Machine gun: 12.7 mm.
Crew: 3.

The RPG-7 is a Russian anti-tank rocket launcher, entered service in 1961.
It is a light, shoulder-fired, reloadable anti-tank rocket launcher.
The launcher tube can fire a wide range of rockets.
The RPG-7 can be equipped with a PGO-7V sight or NSP-2 infrared night sight.
Very widely distributed worldwide, in service in nearly 70 countries.
Crew: 2.

The AT-4 Spigot / 9K111 Fagot is a Russian anti-tank missile, entered service in 1973.
It is wire-guided, semi-automatic, portable by a two-man team.
It consists of the firing post with 9P135 support and 9M111 missile.
The missile is packaged in a tube that serves as launch tube and tactical packaging.
Caliber: 119 mm.
Penetration: 200 mm.
Maximum range: 2000 m.
Minimum firing distance: 70 m.
Adopted by many armies worldwide.
Crew: 2.

The 9K115 Metis or AT-7 Saxhorn is a Soviet/Russian portable company-level anti-tank system,
with wire-guided semi-automatic command, belonging to the second generation of anti-tank missiles (ATGM).
It is designed to engage armored targets, fixed or mobile, as well as fortified points,
visually observable, at distances between 40 and 2000 meters.
Crew: 2.

The SPG-9 (Lance in Russian) is a Soviet heavy anti-tank grenade launcher, entered service in 1963.
This system requires a crew of four men capable of carrying it disassembled (in marching position) over long distances.
Caliber: 73 mm.
Crew: 4.

The MT-12 or 2A-29 is a Soviet 100 mm smoothbore anti-tank gun,
which served as the main towed anti-tank artillery in the Soviet army from the early 1970s to the late 1980s.
It was widely used in the Russo-Ukrainian war.
Caliber: 100 mm.
Crew: 6.

The 2S1 Gvozdika is a Soviet 122 mm self-propelled howitzer.
It is essentially an extended version of the MT-LB, with a 2A-18 (D-30) howitzer mounted on a turret.
Semi-amphibious vehicle, it can also operate in snowstorms and on swamps.
It is protected against NBC effects and has infrared optical vision.
Caliber: 122 mm.
Crew: 4.

The 2S3 Akatsia is a Soviet self-propelled gun designed in the late 1960s, entered service in 1971.
The Akatsia is designed on the GM-123 chassis which is also used by the 2S4 Tyulpan and 2S5 Giatsint-S.
It is compatible with all 152 mm ammunition used by towed guns D-20, ML-20 and D-1.
Still in service in eighteen countries.
Caliber: 152 mm.
Crew: 4.

The 2S5 Giatsint is a Russian 152 mm self-propelled artillery gun, entered service in 1976.
Cannon: 152 mm, 2A37.
Range: 30.5 km.
Rate of fire: 5-6 rounds per minute.
Crew: 5.

The 2S7 Pion is a Russian 203 mm self-propelled artillery gun, entered service in 1975.
It is capable of firing conventional shells and nuclear warhead shells.
Its maximum firing distance is 47 km.
The weapon system is installed on a tracked chassis with seven road wheels.
The running gear is derived from the T-80 tank.
Cannon: 2A44, 203 mm.
Crew: 7 (2S7) / 6 (2S7M).

The PzH 2000 is a German self-propelled artillery gun, entered service in 1998.
It is developed to replace the M109 American-origin self-propelled artillery gun.
It is armed with a 155 mm cannon allowing a firing range of 56 km.
Automatic loading allows a very high rate of fire of 8 to 10 rounds/min.
The PzH 2000 chassis is derived from the German Leopard-2 tank chassis.
Range: 30 km / 56 km self-propelled projectile.
Crew: 5.

The M109 is an American self-propelled artillery gun, entered service in 1963.
It is widely exported worldwide.
Cannon: 155 mm.
Range M109: 14.6 km.
Range M109A5: 22 km / 30 km self-propelled projectile.
Rate of fire: 3-4 rds/min.
Crew: 6 (M109) / 4 (M109A6).

The 2S19 Msta-S is a Russian self-propelled artillery gun, entered service in 1989.
It is armed with a 152 mm 2A65 cannon.
Its chassis is derived from the T-80 tank chassis.
The 2S19 Msta-S is equipped with an ammunition reloading system installed at the rear of the vehicle.
Range: 6.5 km to 24.7 km / 28.5 km self-propelled projectile.
Rate of fire: 8 rounds per minute.
Crew: 5.

The 2S35 Koalitsiya-SV is a Russian self-propelled artillery gun, in development since the early 2010s.
The chassis is derived from the T-90 tank.
For mass production, the 2S35 weapon system will be installed on the Armata chassis.
Cannon: 2A88 152 mm.
Range: 40 km / 70 km self-propelled projectile.
Sustained rate of fire: 10 rounds per minute.
Crew: 3.
The 2S4 Tyulpan is a Russian 240 mm heavy self-propelled mortar.\nCrew: 3.

The PLZ-07 is a Chinese 122 mm self-propelled artillery gun, developed in the 2000s.
It uses the chassis of the ZBD-04 infantry fighting vehicle.
The PLZ-07 has amphibious capability, propelled in water by track movement.
The PLZ-07 is armed with a 122 mm cannon derived from the Soviet D-30 cannon.
Maximum firing distance is 18 km with standard shell and 27 km with propelled ammunition.
Crew: 5.

The 2A-36 Giatsint-B is a medium artillery piece used by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, developed from 1968.
It exists in a self-propelled tracked version without turret 2S5 Giatsint-S.
The 2A-36 is widely used by Ukrainian armed forces since 2014 against Donbass separatists then against Russia.
The Russian army put them back into service in 2022 due to a significant need for artillery pieces.
The cannon is 152 mm caliber and is rifled.
Maximum firing range with standard HE-FRAG shell is 28.5 km and 30 to 33 km.
Crew: 6.

The M101 (105 mm) is an American howitzer from World War II, entered mass production in 1941.
It has been (or still is) in service in the armies of many countries around the world.
Caliber: 105 mm.
Crew: 8.
The D-30 122 mm howitzer is a Soviet field artillery piece considered robust and usable in difficult conditions, entered service in the 1960s.\nCaliber: 122 mm.\nCrew: 6.

The M-46 130 mm gun is a Soviet towed artillery piece from the 1950s,
intended for corps artillery.
Caliber: 130 mm.
Crew: 8.

The 2A65 Msta-B is a Russian/Soviet 152 mm towed howitzer, designed to destroy armored vehicles and fortifications.
Its artillery part has a similar design to that of the 2S19 self-propelled howitzer of the same caliber.
Caliber: 152 mm.
Crew: 6.

The M-777 is an American 155 mm towed howitzer.
It is used by the ground forces of the United States, Australia, Canada, India, Saudi Arabia and Ukraine.
Caliber: 155 mm.
Crew: 7.

The 152 mm gun-howitzer M1955, also known as D-20,
was manufactured in the Soviet Union in the 1950s.
Caliber: 152 mm.
Crew: 8.

The BM-21 Grad is a Russian 122 mm multiple rocket launcher, entered service in 1963.
It has the 6×6 wheeled chassis of the Ural-375D heavy truck.
It is equipped with 40 launch tubes for 122 mm rockets.
Maximum range varies by ammunition type between 14 km and 20.75 km.
The new ammunition range extends firing distance up to 40 km.
Production stopped in 1988.
Crew: 3.

The BM-30 Smerch or 9A52-2 Smerch-M is a 300 mm heavy self-propelled multiple rocket launcher, entered service in 1989.
It is designed to fire a full salvo of 12 solid-propellant projectiles.
This system is intended to neutralize personnel, armor and unprotected targets in concentration areas,
artillery batteries, command posts and ammunition depots.
A program to replace it with the Tornado-S began in 2018.
Crew: 3.

The BM-27 Uragan is a self-propelled multiple rocket launcher system designed in the Soviet Union, entered service in the late 1970s.
It is capable of launching 220 mm rockets from 16 launch tubes mounted at the rear of a ZIL-135 8x8 chassis.
A full salvo of 16 rockets can be fired in 20 seconds and can engage targets within a radius of 35 kilometers.
Crew: 4.
The SCUD-B is an intermediate-range ballistic missile of Russian origin,\ncapable of carrying a nuclear or chemical warhead, with a maximum effective range of 550 km.\nCrew: 3.

The M270 MLRS, Multiple Launch Rocket System, is an American multiple rocket launcher, entered service in 1983.
It is installed on a tracked chassis derived from the M2 Bradley infantry fighting vehicle.
Its cabin is protected against small caliber weapons.
It is equipped with two pods of six 227 mm rockets.
Production stopped in 2003.
Crew: 3.

The RM-70 multiple rocket launcher is a Czechoslovak army version and heavier variant of the BM-21 Grad,
offering superior performance to this area saturation artillery system, introduced in 1971.
The RM-70 replaces the Ural-375D 6x6 truck with a Tatra T813 Kolos 8x8 chassis as the carrier platform
for the 40-rocket launcher.
The new carrier vehicle provides enough space to carry an additional pack of 40 122 mm rockets,
allowing automatic reloading.
Caliber: 122 mm.
Crew: 4.

The 82PM-41 mortar, M-41 or 82 mm mortar model 1941 was a Soviet mortar
of 82 millimeter caliber developed during World War II as an infantry mortar,
with production started in 1941.
Caliber: 82 mm.
Crew: 4.

The LAV-M, Light Armored Vehicle – Mortar, is an American self-propelled mortar, entered service in 1986.
It uses the chassis of the LAV-25 reconnaissance vehicle.
The armament consists of the 81 mm M252 mortar.
For self-defense, the vehicle is equipped with a 7.62 mm M240E1 machine gun mounted on the roof.
Ammunition stock is 99 81 mm mortar shells and 1000 7.62 mm rounds.
Crew: 5.
The MDK-2M is a Soviet army tracked trench excavator vehicle.\nCrew: 2.
The PZM is a Soviet army wheeled trench excavator vehicle.\nCrew: 2.

The GMZ-3 is a Soviet tracked mine layer.
It is designed for mechanized laying of anti-tank, anti-track and anti-bottom mines in soil or snow
on the path of enemy tanks and armored vehicles.
Crew: 3.
The UMZ (Universal Mine Layer) is a Soviet engineering vehicle\nintended for remote mining by projection, built on a ZIL-131 truck base.\nCrew: 3.

The UR-77 \"Meteorit\" is a Soviet combat vehicle, a self-propelled rocket launcher for demining,\ndesigned on the base of the 2S1 \"Gvozdika\" self-propelled howitzer, mass-produced since 1978.\nCrew: 2.

The M136 Volcano (Vehicle-Launched Scatterable Mine System)
is an automated mine laying system developed by the US Army in the 1980s.
The system uses preloaded containers containing multiple anti-personnel (AP) and/or anti-tank (AT) mines,
which are scattered over a wide area when ejected.
Crew: 2.

The KMT-5 is a Soviet tank mine plow from the mid-20th century,
designed for minefield reconnaissance and opening passages.
These breaches then allow movement of armor not equipped with anti-mine devices.
Crew: 2.
The IMR-2 is a Russian engineering tank, introduced in 1982.\nStill in service in Russian armed forces.\nCrew: 2.

The MTU-72 armored bridge layer is a military engineering vehicle designed to deploy an assault bridge,
allowing tanks and other military vehicles to cross trenches and water obstacles,
entered service in 1974.
Crew: 2.

The TMM-3 is designed to establish crossings over obstacles up to 40 meters wide
and up to 3 meters deep, allowing passage of wheeled and tracked vehicles weighing up to 60 tons.
Country: USSR/Russia.
Crew: 3.
The TMM-6 is a Russian bridge-laying vehicle, developed between 1999 and the late 2000s.\nCrew: 3.
The PTS-2 is a Soviet military tracked amphibious transport vehicle\ncapable of carrying vehicles on its deck and transporting them on water like a barge or ferry.\nCrew: 2.

The mined route opening system (SOUVIM) allows securing a route lightly polluted
by anti-tank or anti-personnel mines, detectable or pressure-activated.
It is intended to participate in mobility support missions by ensuring,
over long distances, rapid opening of lightly mined routes (harassment mining)
in 2nd echelon or rear area of major units (logistics flow zone) in a low-intensity conflict.
Crew: 2.
The 1V18 Klyon is a Soviet command vehicle, designed on the BTR-60 chassis.\nCrew: 5.

The 1S91 (NATO code - Straight Flush) is a Soviet-origin long-range mobile air defense radar,
currently in service in Russian armed forces.
Designed to operate with the 2K12 Kub anti-aircraft missile system, it is mounted on a GM-568 tracked chassis.
Crew: 4.
The RQ-7A Shadow 200 is a reconnaissance drone developed by the United States.\nOperators: Australia, United States, Sweden, Romania.\nCrew: 0.
The Su-25 Grach is a ground attack, close air support and anti-tank aircraft developed by the USSR in the 1970s.\nCrew: 1.
The Northrop F-5E is a family of light and maneuverable fighter aircraft, designed and manufactured by Northrop in the United States,\nwith manufacturing beginning in 1962.\nCrew: 1.

The Typhoon is a European fighter aircraft. First flight on March 27, 1994.
The Typhoon entered service in 2004.
It is also known as EF-2000.
It is a twin-engine, multi-role fighter, developed by the Eurofighter consortium,
composed of the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy and Spain.
Cannon: 27 mm, Mauser BK-27.
External pylons: 8 underwing pylons, 5 under fuselage, 9,000 kg of weapons.
Air-to-air missiles: AIM-9 Sidewinder, AIM-120 AMRAAM, AIM-132 AMRAAM.
Air-to-ground missiles: AGM-88 HARM, AGM-65 Maverick, Storm Shadow.
Bombs: Paveway II.
Crew: 1.
Ceiling: 19,800 m.
Range: 1,389 km.
Endurance: 2,900 km, 3,790 km with 3 refuelings.

The 2K12 Kub (NATO code: SA-6 Gainful) is an anti-aircraft weapon system equipped with surface-to-air missiles,
built in more than 500 units between 1968 and 1985.
It operates with a mobile radar, the 1S91.
Crew: 4.
The 9K32 Strela-2, designated by NATO as SA-7 \"Grail\", is a Soviet-designed man-portable surface-to-air missile system,\ninfrared-guided with a high explosive warhead.\nCrew: 1.

The 9K33 Osa (NATO code: SA-8 Gecko) is a highly mobile anti-aircraft vehicle equipped with very short-range surface-to-air missiles,
of Soviet design.
Maximum missile speed according to versions is Mach 2.4,
minimum engagement altitude is 25 meters, maximum effective altitude range is 5,000 meters.
First air defense missile system to incorporate its own engagement radars on a single vehicle.
Crew: 5.

The Franco-German Roland missile is a short-range surface-to-air missile.
The Roland short-range anti-aircraft system is mounted on an armored chassis (AMX-30R for France, Marder for Germany)
or on an air-transportable wheeled cabin.
One of the few foreign missiles purchased by the US Army.
Crew: 3.

The 2S-6 Tunguska (NATO: SA-19 Grison) is a Soviet-origin self-propelled anti-aircraft artillery and surface-to-air missile system,
developed in the 1970s.
Its main role is to protect armored and infantry units against helicopters and ground attack aircraft.
Main users: Russia, India.
Crew: 4.

The AH-64 Apache is an American attack helicopter, entered service in 1984.
The AH-64D Apache Longbow version can receive an AN/APG-78 Longbow millimeter-wave radar installed above the main rotor.
The AH-64E Apache Guardian version is the most modern currently in service.
Cannon: 30 mm M230, capacity 1,200 rounds.
Air-to-ground missiles: up to 16.
Air-to-air missiles: 2.
Rockets: 70 mm.
Widely exported worldwide.
Crew: 2.

The Mi-8 is a Russian multi-role transport helicopter, entered service in 1965.
It gave birth to the Mi-14 Haze with amphibious capability, the Mi-17 and Mi-171 export versions.
The Mi-8 is very widely distributed worldwide.
More than 50 countries use it in their armed forces or in civilian version.
Crew: 3.

The Mi-24 is a Russian attack helicopter, entered service in 1972.
It is designed using many systems from the Mi-8 transport helicopter.
It can receive a wide range of weapons: rockets, missiles and gun pods.
The Mi-24 can carry a group of eight soldiers in the compartment behind the cockpit.
The first Mi-24A version has a three-crew cabin in 1 + 2 configuration.
From the Mi-24B model, it is replaced by a tandem cabin.
The Mi-24 is very widely distributed worldwide.
Nearly sixty countries employ it in their armed forces.
More than 3,500 units have been produced, all models combined.
Machine gun: Yak-B rotary 4 x 12.7 mm.
Cannon: GSh-23L 23 mm / GSh-30K 30 mm.
Rockets: S-5, S-8, S-13, S-24.
Air-to-ground missiles: Shturm-V, Ataka-M.
Air-to-air missiles: Igla-V, R-60M, R-63V.
Crew: 2 + 8 soldiers.
Range: 1000 km.

The Mi-28 is a Russian attack helicopter.
It was developed in the Soviet Union, then in Russia in the 1980s-2000s.
It entered service in 2008 in Mi-28N version.
On August 16, 1996, Mil unveiled the Mi-28N Night Hunter version, capable of night combat.
The Mi-28N is a tandem two-seat helicopter intended for attack and anti-tank combat missions.
In 2012, Iraq ordered fifteen Mi-28N delivered in 2014-2016. In March 2014, Algeria ordered forty-two Mi-28N.
Versions: Mi-28 / Mi-28N / Mi-28NE / Mi-28UB / Mi-28NM.
Cannon: 2A42 30 mm.
Rockets: S-8, S-13.
Air-to-ground missiles: Shturm-V, Ataka-V.
Air-to-air missiles: Igla-V.
Crew: 2.
Range: 450 km.

The Ka-50 Black Shark (Hokum-A in NATO designation) is a Russian reconnaissance and attack helicopter.
It was developed in the Soviet Union in the 1980s.
First flight on June 17, 1982. The Ka-50 entered service in 1995.
Crew: 1.

The UH-1, better known as Huey, is an American military helicopter, deployed in Vietnam from 1963.
Hueys were used for medical evacuations (MedEvac), command and control,
air assaults, troop and equipment transport, and as armed gunships.
Crew: 2 + 11.

The UH-60 Black Hawk is an American multi-role transport helicopter, entered service in 1979.
It is derived into numerous versions: for Special Forces, navalized for the Navy,
for the Coast Guard, search and rescue missions, medical evacuation,
VIP transport and versions for transporting specific equipment:
radar, C3 Command-Control-Communication, weapons.
Produced in more than four thousand units for about thirty countries worldwide.
Crew: 2 + 11.
